newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nissan races to catch up to rivals in RV market.
newsitem.headline: Nissan races to catch up to rivals in RV market.

text.p: Nissan Motor Co, racing to reflate its shrinking market share and catch up with rivals in the booming recreational vehicle market, said on Thursday it was planning its biggest capital spending hike in seven years.
Drawing from savings made possible by cost-cutting efforts and the weaker yen, Japan's second-biggest car maker said it would invest more heavily in developing new models.
"We must invest to develop new technologies and equipment that will help raise our market share in the future," a Nissan spokesman said.

The company intends to boost capital investment by nearly 38 percent in the business year beginning in April 1997 to around 110 billion yen ($894 million), up from a planned 80 billion yen ($650 million) in 1996/97.

Until the 1996/97 business year, Nissan reduced its capital investment for six years in a row after spending a record 318.6 billion yen ($2.59 billion) in 1990/91, just about when Japan's "bubble era" of inflated stock and asset prices began to pop.
The strong yen in the early 1990s also compelled the firm to cut back, but the yen's steady decline against the dollar in the past two years has encouraged Nissan to shift back into forward gear.
Nissan's parent current profit is expected to rise 47 percent in 1996/97 to 80 billion yen ($650 million), partly helped by the weaker yen's boost to exports.
Nissan's domestic market share fell to a record-low 20.8 percent in calendar 1996, due to slow development of new recreational vehicle models, sales of which are booming in Japan.
Recreational vehicles include station wagons, sport-utility vehicles and minivans.

"Nissan must think that it should boost its investment in product improvements and that it won't be able to survive in two or three years without making large investments. But 100 billion may not be enough to make good models," said senior analyst Nobuaki Yanachi of Kankaku Research.
He said Nissan would also need to decide how much to raise its research-and-development expenditure.

Nissan, which has been lagging rivals such as Honda Motor Co and Toyota Motor Corp in the development of recreational vehicles, said the extra funds would allow it to roll out new models more quickly and to be more responsive to market trends.

"Engine development is important. Nissan had a big hit in the past (1994 and 1995) with its Cefiro model equipped with the newly developed VQ engine. It (new technology) can lure consumers," Yanachi said. Nissan developed the VQ engine,which it says is quieter and more powerful than conventional engines.

Mitsubishi Motors Corp has developed a GDI (gasoline direct injection) engine for some of its medium-sized cars and consumers have been eager to buy them because of their fuel efficiency and low emissions.

The Nissan spokesman said the firm would continue to boost investment in order to achieve a market share of 25 percent by 2000. But Kankaku's Yanachi said it would be difficult for it to achieve this target.
"It is very tough for a full-line carmaker like Nissan, which produces a wide range of models from minicars to luxury sedans, to raise its market share amid stiff competition."
Nissan recently said it had developed a new production system that will cut vehicle development time by 40 percent to just 19 months.

The capital investment in 1997/98 will include funds to create a system to exchange information on computer-aided design (CAD) and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) between Nissan's technical centre and its domestic plants.
Nissan said the move was expected to cut development costs. ($1=123 yen)
